title: Exchanging robes
hookLine: the Buddha gives Kassapa his worn rag robes and takes Kassapa's soft patchwork cloak (SN 16.11)

cards: Years later, an old monk tells Ananda about the day he met the Buddha. He's not in a sentimental mood; he's making a point. But the story is tender anyway.

He'd left home, he says, already wearing a robe, and set out looking for a teacher. On the road between Rajagaha and Nalanda, at a shrine by the way, he saw the Buddha sitting, and knew at once: this is my teacher.
What happened next involved two pieces of cloth.

teach.h: A CLOAK FOLDED INTO A SEAT.
teach.b: First, the seat. In the discourse, Kassapa bows and declares himself the Buddha's disciple. They walk on together, and the Buddha steps off the road to sit at the foot of a tree.
Kassapa folds his own outer robe, a patchwork cloak, and lays it down as a seat. Second, the remark.
The Buddha sits and says, in effect: this patchwork cloak of yours is soft. That's all, a comment about cloth. Kassapa hears what's underneath it and offers the cloak as a gift.

teach.h: WILL YOU WEAR MY RAG ROBES?
teach.b: The Buddha accepts, and asks a question back: will you wear my rag robes, the worn-out hempen ones? These are robes made from cloth other people threw away. Kassapa says yes.
The teacher takes the soft cloak; the student takes the rough, worn one. Fourth, what Kassapa makes of it.

Telling the story to Ananda, he says that if anyone could rightly be called the Buddha's true son, heir to his worn rag robes, it would be him. Not heir to a throne or a teaching hall. Heir to his old clothes.
Kassapa treasured the worn one because of whose it had been, and what it said: a life with few wants, chosen on purpose.

how: In some Theravada forest monasteries monks still sew robes from donated or cast-off cloth and dye them by hand, and the story of the exchanged robes is told as the bond between the Buddha and Mahakassapa.

o: Kassapa's cloak traded for the Buddha's rag robes
trading robes to mark a monk's rise in rank
a yearly gift of new robes from lay people

the one Kassapa tells the story to

he only remarked that it was soft; Kassapa offered it.

games.q: the Buddha has just said your patchwork cloak is soft. what do you do?
o: fold it away so no one sits on it.
games.why: Kassapa offers it, and the Buddha asks him to wear his worn rag robes in return.

practice: Rest a hand on whatever you're wearing and feel the cloth: new or old, chosen to impress or chosen because it was clean.

Then picture something you own that's worn, faded or mended, the thing you'd usually leave in the drawer, and imagine walking out the door in it, the way Kassapa did. Notice what that stirs up, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Exchanging robes. Kassapa offers his soft patchwork cloak, and the Buddha gives him his own worn rag robes in return. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali pamsukula: a rag robe, sewn from cloth others threw away, like the robes Kassapa received.

carryVoice: Your line: the worn robe. The soft cloak is the easy thing to want. Day seven hundred forty.
